docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This subsystem monitors environmental conditions using digital sensors for soil moisture, rainwater, and temperature/humidity. It uses a Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller to read sensor data via analog pins and digital I/O and PWM which processes the information and makes it available to the rest of the system for decision-making.

The system is powered by a 9V, 3A unregulated power supply and is regulated down to 5V, 1.5A using a voltage regulator to ensure safe and stable operation of the microcontroller and all connected sensors.

It interfaces with three digital sensors: -Soil Moisture Sensor -Rain Water Sensor -Temperature/Humidity Sensor

Actuator Interface: This subsystem doesn't directly control an actuator but it provides sensor data to other subsystems such as motor control that can act upon the readings.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text: Subsystem board powered from 9 V input through a 5 V regulator. Includes a microcontroller connected to: - Analog soil moisture sensor - Temperature/humidity sensor - Rain sensor - 8-pin connector to communicate with other boards

docs.title: Soil Moisture Sensor (Analog)
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1: Resistive probe (e.g., YL-69 Module)$2 eachYL-69 Resistive Sensor Very low costEasy analog output for ADC Corrodes quicklyNon-linear readingsRequires frequent calibration Option 2: Capacitive soil moisture sensor v1.2$5 eachCapacitive Soil Module No corrosionStable analog signalCompact size Slightly higher costNeeds calibration per soil type Option 3: Industrial analog soil moisture transmitter (4–20 mA output)$22 eachIndustrial Soil Transmitter Weatherproof housingHighly accurate and robust ExpensiveLarger form factor

Choice: Option 2 — Capacitive Soil Moisture Sensor v1.2 Rationale: Provides stable analog readings without corrosion, making it suitable for long-term outdoor testing while staying low-cost and easy to integrate with the microcontroller’s ADC.

docs.title: Temperature & Humidity Sensor
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1: DHT22 / AM2302$6 eachDHT22 Sensor Low costEasy to use (Arduino library) Slow sampling rate±2 °C, ±5 % RH accuracy Option 2: SHT31-D (I²C)$12 eachSHT31-D Sensor High accuracy (±2 % RH, ±0.3 °C)Fast responseI²C communication Higher price Option 3: BME280 (I²C/SPI)$14 eachBME280 Sensor Adds pressure measurementAccurate & low power Adds unnecessary feature (pressure)Slightly more expensive

Choice: Option 2 — SHT31-D Sensor Rationale: Best balance of precision, low power, and easy I²C integration for microcontroller communication.

docs.title: Rain Sensor
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1: Analog rain detection board (YL-83)$3 eachYL-83 Rain Module Cheap and simpleAnalog or digital output Corrosion over timeNot weatherproof Option 2: Optical rain sensor (IR reflection type)$25 eachOptical Rain Sensor Non-contact detectionLong life Requires optical calibrationHigher cost Option 3: Tipping-bucket rain gauge$60 eachTipping Bucket Sensor Accurate rainfall measurement (mm) Bulky, mechanical partsRequires mounting and calibration

Choice: Option 1 — YL-83 Analog Rain Module Rationale: Simple analog detection is sufficient for moisture-triggered irrigation feedback without needing quantitative rainfall measurement.

docs.title: Voltage Regulator (9 V → 5 V)
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1: LM7805 Linear Regulator$1 eachLM7805 Simple circuit, low noiseStable 5 V output Inefficient (heat loss) Option 2: LM2596 Buck Converter$4 eachLM2596 Buck Module Efficient, handles higher currentCool operation More electrical noise (may affect ADC)

Choice: Option 1 — LM7805 Linear Regulator Rationale: System current is low (<150 mA), so heat dissipation is minimal. The LM7805’s clean output benefits analog sensors and simplifies the PCB design.
